The turning and steering for these models are great. But it's unusable because the lane centering is so bad. Left wheels were always on the lane lines.

I wonder if there's some assumption in the models on how wide the vehicle is - training data?   Fairly consistently, when I read folks saying a model hugs left, it's well-centered for me, and a model that's centered hugs right for me.   My vehicle is 6 ft. wide from the outer edges of the tires.   I have tried moving the C3X around the windshield, mainly horizontally, and after (re)calibrating it appears to drive - here in terms of intra-lane placement, exactly the same whether a few inches to the right or left of center.   I can only temporarily get it to drive e.g. more towards the center by gently pushing on the left edge of the C3X to slightly cant it to the right (expected).

That is interesting. The thing that I don't understand is how it can not be corrected for, I get that the models won't be perfect, but it knows where it is in the lane it knows how close it is to each lane side, so I don't get why it can't be corrected for and just find the center based on how close it is to each line.

OP used to steer more heuristically (like you suggest), and lane bias adjustments were available, at least in forks like Sunnypilot.  These days it's an end-to-end neural net model - effectively a black box with (encoded visual camera) data in and driving control inputs out.   Today's approach has great theoretical promise, though the model has to be large enough and trained with sufficient, diverse data to be able to generalize well over variations in lane and vehicle width, the appearance of curves etc.   We're all participating in a big trial-and-error experiment.
Does make me wonder though why some models center fine on some cars but not others.
